title: Women Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development
subtitle: Diagnose your existing business, run it on real numbers and grow it with a funded, realistic 90-day plan.
description: For women who already sell something and want a stronger, more profitable business. You will learn to diagnose your business stage, learn from real customers, cost full orders, set quality standards, track a monthly dashboard, fund growth safely and hand over work so the business does not depend on you alone.
outcomes: Diagnose your business stage and name its main growth limit using your own numbers
Run customer discovery conversations and write an evidence-based customer profile
Cost and quote a full order that protects your margin, including your time and payment fees
Track six key numbers monthly and act on the weakest one
Compare growth options with payback and loan affordability tests and choose a safe funding source
Write a 90-day growth plan with a SMART goal, weekly actions and a delegation plan
audience: Women in Nigeria and across Africa who already run a small business and want to grow it with discipline.
tools: A smartphone with WhatsApp and a calculator
A notebook and pen, or Google Sheets on your phone
One to three months of your sales and cost records, even rough ones
Access to your bank or wallet app transaction history

modules.title: Know Where You Stand: Stage, Customers and Business Model
modules.overview: You start by diagnosing your business honestly: which stage it is in, what is holding it back, who really buys and why, and how all the parts fit on one page. These three lessons give you the evidence you need before you spend money on growth.

lessons.title: Survival, stable or ready to grow: diagnosing your business stage
objectives: Place your business in one of three stages using simple signs
Calculate your monthly profit and your profit per working hour
Identify the single biggest limit on your growth: demand, capacity, cash or time
Name the barriers women owners often face and one way to reduce each

blocks.text: Many women in Nigeria already run a business: a food stall, a tailoring shop, a hair salon, a poultry pen, a small provisions store. This course is for you if you are already selling and want the business to become stronger, more organised and more profitable. We will not start from zero. We will start by looking honestly at where your business stands today.
Three stages of a small business

Business advisers often describe small firms in stages. The names vary, but the idea is simple. At the **survival** stage, money comes in and goes out the same day, and the owner is not sure whether she made a profit. At the **stable** stage, sales are fairly regular, the owner knows her main costs and the business pays her something every month. At the **growth-ready** stage, the business is stable, demand is bigger than what she can currently supply, and she has the records to prove it. Growth spent at the wrong stage often fails: a loan taken at survival stage usually feeds the household, not the business.

blocks.title: Build each stage on the one below
items: Growth-ready: proven extra demand
Stable: regular sales, known costs
Survival: daily cash, no records
blocks.caption: You cannot safely skip a level: growth sits on top of stability, and stability sits on records.

head: Sign
Survival
Stable
Growth-ready
rows: None, or only in her head
Monthly profit known for at least 3 months
Separate account and a small cash reserve
Regular buyers plus orders she has to refuse

blocks.text: Find your real profit and your profit per hour

Profit is what is left after **all** business costs, not the money in your hand at the end of the day. To judge your stage, add up one month of sales, subtract one month of costs, then divide the profit by the hours you worked. Profit per hour tells you whether the business is paying you fairly for your time, which matters a great deal for women who also carry most of the cooking, childcare and caring at home.

blocks.title: Worked example: Aisha's small chops business
blocks.context: For example, Aisha makes puff-puff, samosa and spring rolls for parties in Kaduna. She wrote down every sale and cost for four weeks. Figures are illustrative and prices are approximate.
steps: Monthly costs (flour, oil, fillings, packs, gas, transport): ₦128,000.
Hours worked on the business, counted from her diary: 70 hours.
Profit per hour: ₦63,000 divided by 70 = ₦900 per hour.
She also noticed she refused 3 party orders because her single fryer could not cook fast enough.
blocks.result: Aisha is stable: she knows her numbers and makes a profit. Her limit is capacity (one fryer), not demand, because customers are already asking for more than she can make. That points to a very different growth move from someone whose limit is too few customers.

blocks.text: What is really holding you back?

items: **Demand**: not enough people buying. Fix with customer research and better selling (Lesson 1.2).
**Capacity**: you cannot make or deliver more. Fix with equipment, a helper or a better process (Module 3).
**Cash**: you cannot buy stock or inputs in advance. Fix with deposits, tighter credit and planned funding (Lessons 2.1 and 3.1).
**Time**: you are the bottleneck for every task. Fix with delegation and routines (Lesson 3.2).

blocks.name: businesswoman
blocks.alt: A woman business owner standing confidently with a folder
blocks.caption: Diagnosing your stage and your main limit is the first decision of a growing owner.

blocks.text: Barriers many women owners face

The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals include **Goal 5**, gender equality, which calls for women to have equal rights to economic resources and financial services, and **Goal 8**, decent work and economic growth, which encourages the growth and formalisation of micro and small enterprises. These goals exist because women commonly face extra barriers in business. You may recognise some of them:

head: Barrier
How it shows up
One practical response
rows: Business hours are broken up by cooking, school runs and caring
Block fixed business hours and share home tasks where possible
Business cash is used for family needs
Separate account and a fixed weekly pay for yourself
Banks ask for land or property she does not hold
Build records and use cooperatives or group lending
Travel to markets or clients is risky or costly
Delivery partners, daytime meetings, sharing location with family
Price from your costs, then hold the price politely

blocks.title: Your hours count
blocks.text: If your profit per hour is lower than what a helper would cost per hour, the business is quietly using your free labour. That is not a failure. It is information: it tells you where to focus first.

Before the next lesson, collect one month of sales and costs, even if they are rough. Use a notebook or a simple phone note. Estimate your hours honestly. These numbers are the base for everything else in this course.

takeaways: Growth spent at survival stage usually leaks into the household.
Profit is sales minus all costs; divide it by your hours to see if the business pays you fairly.
Name your main limit: demand, capacity, cash or time, because each needs a different fix.
Women often face extra barriers such as care work and lack of collateral; plan around them deliberately.

activity.title: Diagnose your business stage
steps: Write down your total sales and total costs for the last four weeks.
Calculate profit and divide it by your estimated working hours.
Use the stage table to tick the signs that match your business.
Write one sentence naming your main limit (demand, capacity, cash or time) and the evidence for it.
activity.evidence: A photo of your one-page stage diagnosis with the profit-per-hour calculation.

lessons.title: Customer discovery: interviewing real buyers and writing a customer profile
objectives: Plan 10 to 15 short customer conversations
Ask questions about past behaviour instead of opinions
Tally answers to find patterns you can trust
Write a one-paragraph customer profile with evidence

blocks.text: Most owners describe their customers as "everybody". In practice, a small group of people brings most of your money, and they buy for specific reasons. **Customer discovery** means talking to real buyers to find out who they are, what problem you solve for them, and what makes them choose you or leave you. It costs almost nothing except your time.
Ask about the past, not the future

People are polite. If you ask "Would you buy my new product?" most will say yes and never buy. The book *The Mom Test* by Rob Fitzpatrick explains a better approach: ask about what people **actually did** recently, avoid pitching your idea, and listen for specific details such as dates, amounts and alternatives they used. Past behaviour is the best evidence of future behaviour.

head: Weak question (opinion)
Strong question (past behaviour)
rows: The last time you used a laundry, what happened?
How much did you spend on this last month?
What did you do the last time your clothes came back late?
Have you told anyone about us? What did you say?

blocks.title: From conversations to a customer profile
items: Choose who to talk to
Ask about past behaviour
Write notes the same day
Tally the patterns
Write the profile
blocks.caption: Discovery is a short, repeatable process, not a one-time survey.

blocks.text: Who to talk to

items: **Your best regular customers**: they tell you what you do well.
**Customers who stopped buying**: they tell you what went wrong.
**People who buy from a competitor**: they tell you what you are missing.
Aim for 10 to 15 conversations of about 10 minutes each, in person, on a call or by WhatsApp voice note.

blocks.name: interview
blocks.alt: Two people sitting and talking in a conversation
blocks.caption: A short, respectful conversation with a real buyer beats any guess about the market.

blocks.text: Six questions that work

items: "Tell me about the last time you bought [this kind of product or service]."
"What was the hardest or most annoying part?"
"What did you do about it? Did you try anyone else?"
"Roughly how much do you spend on this in a month?"
"Why did you choose us, and what nearly made you choose someone else?"
"Who else do you know who has this problem?"

blocks.title: Respect people's data
blocks.text: Ask permission before you save someone's phone number or quote them. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 expects businesses to collect only the personal data they need, for a clear purpose, and to keep it secure. Do not share customers' numbers or screenshots of their chats with anyone.

blocks.title: Worked example: Blessing's laundry interviews
blocks.context: For example, Blessing runs a wash-and-iron service in Port Harcourt. Sales were flat, so she spoke to 12 people in two weeks: 7 regular customers, 2 who had stopped using her and 3 who used a dry-cleaner nearby.
steps: She wrote short notes after each conversation and tallied repeated answers.
8 of the 12 worked in offices or banks and had no time to wash on weekdays: 8 ÷ 12 = 67 percent.
7 of the 12 said late return was their biggest frustration: 7 ÷ 12 = 58 percent.
Both former customers had left after clothes came back a day late before an important event.
Only 2 people mentioned price at all; the 3 dry-cleaner users already paid more than Blessing charges.
5 people said they would happily pay for pickup and drop-off at their office.
blocks.result: Blessing learned that her real customer is a busy office worker who values reliable timing more than a low price. Her growth idea changed from "cut prices" to "guarantee 48-hour return with office pickup".

blocks.text: Write your customer profile

A customer profile is a short paragraph, backed by your tally, that answers: **who** buys (age range, work, location), **what problem** they have, **what they used before**, **why they choose you**, **what would make them leave**, and **where you can reach** more people like them. Keep the numbers from your tally beside each claim so you can check it later.
How many conversations is enough?

You are not running a national survey. You are looking for patterns. After about 8 to 10 conversations with similar customers, answers usually start to repeat. If every conversation still tells you something completely new, your customers may be more varied than you thought, so keep going or split them into two groups, for example households and shops, and write a short profile for each.

Blessing's profile reads: "Office and bank staff aged about 25 to 45 in our area, with no time to wash on weekdays. Their main frustration is late return (7 of 12). They choose us because we are close and careful with fabrics. They leave when we miss a deadline. We can reach more of them through office receptionists and WhatsApp status." One paragraph like this guides your pricing, marketing and growth plan.

takeaways: Ask about what people did, not what they think they might do.
Talk to best customers, lost customers and competitors' customers.
Tally answers; a pattern from 12 real people beats a guess.
Your customer profile names who, what problem, why you, why they leave and where to reach them.

activity.title: Run five discovery conversations
steps: List 5 people to talk to: at least 3 regular customers and 1 lost customer.
Ask permission, then use the six questions; do not pitch or defend.
Write notes the same day in a notebook or phone note.
Tally answers that appear more than once and write a draft customer profile.
activity.evidence: Your tally sheet and a one-paragraph draft customer profile with numbers beside each claim.

lessons.title: Your one-page business model and an honest readiness check
objectives: Fill in the nine blocks of the Business Model Canvas for your business
Spot weak or missing blocks that limit growth
Score your business on a 20-point readiness checklist
Choose the two lowest-scoring areas to fix first

blocks.text: Once you know your stage and your customer, you need a picture of the whole business on one page. The **Business Model Canvas**, created by Alexander Osterwalder and published by Strategyzer, is a widely used one-page tool for this. It has nine blocks. You can draw it on a sheet of paper in ten minutes.

head: Block
Question it answers
rows: Who are my most important customers?
What problem do I solve or what need do I meet for them?
How do customers find me, buy and receive the product?
How do I keep them coming back?
What do they pay for, how much and how?
What equipment, skills, money or space do I need?
What must I do well every week?
Which suppliers or partners do I rely on?

blocks.name: business-plan
blocks.alt: A person standing beside a large planning board
blocks.caption: The canvas puts your whole business on one page so weak spots become visible.

blocks.title: Worked example: Titi's egg business canvas
blocks.context: For example, Titi keeps about 500 laying hens behind her house near Ibadan and sells crates of eggs. Her canvas, written in a notebook, looks like this.
steps: Customer Segments: two bakeries, one hotel kitchen, about 20 households and 3 market retailers.
Value Propositions: fresh eggs delivered twice a week, consistent size, honest crate count.
Channels: WhatsApp orders, delivery by a hired keke, collection from her gate.
Customer Relationships: personal calls, a WhatsApp broadcast list, credit for the hotel.
Revenue Streams: crates of eggs, plus spent hens sold at the end of the laying cycle.
Key Resources: hens, pen, feeders and drinkers, her own knowledge, a helper.
Key Activities: feeding, cleaning, egg collection and grading, vaccinations, delivery.
Key Partnerships: feed supplier, a veterinary adviser, the keke rider.
Cost Structure: feed is by far the largest cost, then labour, vaccines and transport.
blocks.result: Two weak spots stand out. Almost all revenue depends on feed prices she cannot control, and the hotel's credit means her cash arrives late. These become her first things to fix.

blocks.text: The 20-point readiness check
Score each statement 0 (not true), 1 (partly true) or 2 (fully true). Be honest; nobody else needs to see it. A score shows where to start, not whether you are a good business owner.

blocks.title: Growth readiness checklist
items: Records kept for 3 months
Business money kept separate
Unit cost known per product
Customer profile written
Cash reserve for one month
blocks.caption: Five of the ten checks; the full list is below and each scores 0, 1 or 2.

items: 1. I have written records of sales and costs for at least three months.
2. Business money is kept separate from household money.
3. I know the full cost of each main product or service, including my time.
4. My prices cover my costs and leave a profit.
5. I have a written customer profile based on real conversations.
6. At least half of my sales come from repeat customers.
7. I have enough cash to run the business for one month if sales stop.
8. I know which registration or permits apply to me (CAC, NAFDAC, local levies).
9. Someone else can run key tasks for a day if I am away.
10. I have one written goal for the next three months.

blocks.title: Worked example: Titi's readiness score
blocks.context: For example, Titi scores her egg business honestly.
steps: Fully true (2 points each): statements 1, 2 and 6 = 6 points.
Partly true (1 point each): statements 3, 4, 8, 9 and 10 = 5 points.
Not true (0 points): statements 5 and 7 = 0 points.
Total: 6 + 5 + 0 = 11 out of 20.
blocks.result: Titi's lowest areas are a missing customer profile and no cash reserve. She decides to interview her customers this month and to start setting aside part of each week's profit until she holds one month of feed money.

blocks.title: Read your score
blocks.text: Under 8: focus on records and separating money before anything else. 8 to 14: fix your two lowest items over the next month. 15 and above: you are probably ready to plan a growth move, which we cover in Module 3.
How the blocks connect

The canvas is useful because the blocks depend on each other. If you change one block, check the others. When Titi adds hotels as a customer segment, her channels change (she needs scheduled delivery), her customer relationships change (credit and invoices), her key activities change (grading eggs by size) and her cost structure changes (more transport). A change that looks small on one block can add costs elsewhere, so update the whole page before you decide.
Keep your canvas and score in one folder or one phone album. You will update both at the end of the course, and the change between the two versions becomes part of your final project.

takeaways: The Business Model Canvas shows all nine parts of your business on one page.
Weak blocks, such as one dominant cost or one risky customer, show you what to fix.
A 20-point readiness score points to your two most urgent improvements.
Save your first canvas and score to compare at the end of the course.

activity.title: Draw your canvas and score your readiness
steps: Draw nine boxes on one sheet and label them with the block names.
Fill each block in short phrases about your real business.
Circle the two weakest blocks.
Score the ten readiness statements and add up your total.
Write the two lowest-scoring items and one action for each.
activity.evidence: A photo of your completed canvas and your readiness score sheet.

quiz.q: Aisha's sales were ₦191,000 and her costs ₦128,000 for a month in which she worked 70 hours. What was her profit per hour?
quiz.explain: Profit is ₦191,000 minus ₦128,000 = ₦63,000. Dividing ₦63,000 by 70 hours gives ₦900 per hour.

quiz.q: A business owner refuses several orders each month because her oven is too small, even though she has plenty of customers. What is her main growth limit?
options: Demand
Time
Capacity
Cash
quiz.explain: Customers are already asking for more. The limit is how much she can produce, which is capacity.

quiz.q: Which interview question gives the most reliable evidence?
options: Would you buy this if I made it?
Do you think my price is fair?
Do you like my new packaging?
The last time you bought this, what did you pay and where?
quiz.explain: Questions about what someone actually did recently give facts. Opinions about the future are often polite guesses.

quiz.q: In Blessing's interviews, 7 of 12 people named late return as their main frustration. What should she conclude?
options: Reliable timing matters more to her customers than a lower price
She must cut her prices at once
She should stop serving office workers
The sample is useless because it is less than 100 people
quiz.explain: A clear pattern across 12 real conversations is useful evidence, and price was rarely mentioned. Timing is the problem to solve.

quiz.q: Titi scores 11 out of 20 on the readiness check, with zeros for 'customer profile' and 'cash reserve'. What is the best next step?
options: Take a large loan to double her flock
Ignore the score and focus on social media
Fix the two lowest areas before planning a big growth move
Stop keeping records because they take time
quiz.explain: A middle score means she should strengthen her weakest areas first. Growth on a weak base adds risk.

modules.title: Run It Well: Order Costing, Quality Standards and a Monthly Dashboard
modules.overview: This module turns good intentions into routines. You will cost and quote a full customer order, set quality and safety standards that others can follow, and track a small set of numbers every month so you can see real progress instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Costing and quoting a full order: inputs, your time, delivery and payment fees
objectives: List every cost line in a customer order, including your own time
Calculate a quote that protects a target profit margin
Include payment fees in the price instead of absorbing them
Set a deposit that covers what you must buy before the job

blocks.text: Growing businesses increasingly sell by **order**: a party tray, a set of uniforms, 30 crates of eggs for a hotel, a month of office laundry. An order has costs that a single item on a table does not show: delivery, extra packaging, a helper for the day, payment fees and, very often, your own long hours. If you quote from habit, a big order can make you busy and poorer at the same time.
The six cost lines of an order

items: **Direct inputs**: ingredients, fabric, feed, detergent: everything that goes into the product.
**Packaging**: packs, bags, labels, crates.
**Shared running costs**: the order's fair share of gas, electricity or fuel for a generator.
**Delivery**: transport to the customer, including the return trip.
**Labour**: helpers, plus **your own hours** at a fair rate (decide one, for example ₦1,000 per hour).
**Payment costs**: gateway or POS charges and transfer fees, usually a percentage of the price.

blocks.title: Building an order quote
items: Count direct inputs
Add packaging and shared costs
Add delivery and labour
Choose target margin
Allow for payment fees
Quote and take deposit
blocks.caption: Each step adds a cost you can see, so nothing is forgotten when you name the price.

blocks.text: From cost to quote: the margin formula

**Margin** is profit as a share of the selling price. If you want a 25 percent margin, the cost must be 75 percent of the price. So: **price = total cost ÷ (1 minus target margin)**. If a payment fee is charged as a percentage of the price, subtract it too: **price = total cost ÷ (1 minus margin minus fee rate)**. Doing this protects your margin, because the fee grows with the price.

blocks.title: Worked example: Aisha quotes 50 party packs
blocks.context: For example, a client in Kaduna asks Aisha for 50 small chops packs for a birthday. The client will pay through a payment link. Prices are approximate and for illustration only; check your own supplier and gateway rates.
steps: Ingredients (flour, oil, meat, vegetables, spices): ₦38,500.
Packaging: 50 packs × ₦250 = ₦12,500.
Gas share ₦4,000, delivery to the venue ₦5,000, one helper for the day ₦5,000.
Aisha's own time: 10 hours × ₦1,000 = ₦10,000.
Target margin 25 percent, payment link fee assumed at 1.5 percent: 75,000 ÷ (1 − 0.25 − 0.015) = 75,000 ÷ 0.735 = about ₦102,041.
She rounds to ₦2,050 per pack: 50 × ₦2,050 = ₦102,500.
blocks.result: Aisha quotes ₦102,500 for 50 packs. If she had quoted ₦1,800 per pack from habit (₦90,000), her profit after the fee would have been about ₦13,650, roughly half, for exactly the same work.

blocks.name: deliveries
blocks.alt: A delivery person carrying packages to a customer
blocks.caption: Delivery is a real cost of every order, so it belongs in the quote, not in your pocket.

blocks.text: Deposits protect your cash

For orders, ask for a deposit that at least covers what you must buy in advance. In Aisha's case, ingredients and packaging cost ₦51,000, so a 50 percent deposit of ₦51,250 covers them. Put your terms in writing, even in a WhatsApp message: the quantity, price, delivery date and time, deposit, when the balance is due, and what happens if the client cancels late.

blocks.title: Fake payment alerts
blocks.text: Never release goods because of an SMS or a screenshot. Confirm every payment inside your own bank or wallet app (for example your bank app, Opay or Moniepoint) before delivery. Scammers send convincing fake credit alerts, especially on large orders.
When the client asks for a discount
Quoting service work by time

If you sell a service such as tailoring, hair styling, cleaning or tutoring, most of the cost is time. Work out an **hourly cost** first: add your monthly fixed costs (rent, power, phone data, equipment repairs) and the pay you want for yourself, then divide by the hours you can really sell in a month. For example, ₦60,000 fixed costs plus ₦90,000 owner pay = ₦150,000; divided by 100 sellable hours, that is ₦1,500 an hour. A job that takes 4 hours with ₦2,000 of materials costs 4 × ₦1,500 + ₦2,000 = ₦8,000 before profit and fees.

Before you agree, work out what the discount does to your profit. A 10 percent discount on ₦102,500 is ₦10,250, which removes about 40 percent of Aisha's ₦25,962 profit. Offer something that costs you less instead: free delivery when the client collects nearby, or a smaller pack size at a lower total. Payment fees and gateway rates change, so check your provider's current price list every few months.

takeaways: An order has six cost lines; your own time and payment fees are the ones most often forgotten.
Price = total cost ÷ (1 − target margin − fee rate) protects your margin.
Ask for a deposit that covers what you must buy before the job.
Confirm payments in your own app, never by SMS or screenshot.

activity.title: Quote one real order
steps: Pick a recent or typical order from your own business.
List all six cost lines with your best estimates.
Choose a target margin and your payment fee rate, then calculate the quote.
Write the WhatsApp message with price, deposit, delivery date and cancellation terms.
activity.evidence: Your costing sheet and the written quote message (as a screenshot or note).

lessons.title: Quality standards, safety and fair treatment as you grow
objectives: Write a simple quality standard that a helper can follow
Measure your complaint rate and use a complaint log
Apply core safety practices for food, heat, electricity and money
Treat customers and workers fairly and protect their data

blocks.text: When you do everything yourself, quality lives in your hands and your head. As soon as a helper joins, or orders double, quality depends on whether your standard is **written down** and **checked**. Customers forgive a small business many things, but not unreliable quality. In Lesson 1.2, Blessing learned that late return was the main reason customers left her laundry.
Write a one-page quality standard

items: List the steps of your main product or service in order.
For each step, write what "good" looks like in a way anyone can check: a time, a weight, a count, a photo.
Mark the two or three steps where mistakes cost the most.
Add a final check before anything leaves your hands.
Train your helper with the sheet, then watch them do it once.

blocks.title: Quality without and with a written standard
items: Without a standard
With a standard
blocks.caption: A written standard lets quality survive when you are not standing beside the work.

blocks.text: Track your complaint rate

Keep a **complaint log**: date, customer, what went wrong, what you did, and the cause. Then calculate the **complaint rate**: complaints divided by orders or items, times 100. A number lets you see whether a change really worked.

blocks.title: Worked example: Blessing's laundry standard
blocks.context: For example, Blessing logged complaints for a month, then introduced a written standard: every bag tagged with the customer's name and promised return date, a fabric check before washing, and a count of items on drop-off and on return.
steps: Month 1: 240 items processed, 6 complaints. Rate = 6 ÷ 240 × 100 = 2.5 percent.
Four of the six were late returns and two were missing items.
Month 2 (with the standard): 300 items, 3 complaints. Rate = 3 ÷ 300 × 100 = 1 percent.
No item went missing in Month 2 because items were counted in and out.
blocks.result: Blessing's complaint rate fell from 2.5 percent to 1 percent while volume rose by 60 items. The written standard, not extra effort from Blessing, made the difference.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking items on a large checklist
blocks.caption: A short written checklist keeps quality steady as your team and orders grow.

blocks.text: Safety basics for a growing business

head: Area
Recognised practice
rows: Follow the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, use safe water and raw materials.
Cook in a ventilated space, check hoses and regulators for leaks with soapy water, keep a fire blanket or extinguisher nearby, and never leave hot oil unattended.
Do not overload sockets, keep irons and appliances away from water, unplug when not in use, and site generators outdoors away from doors and windows because exhaust fumes can kill.
Confirm payments in your own app, never share OTPs or PINs, and bank cash daily instead of keeping large amounts at the shop.
If you make food, drinks or cosmetics for sale, check what NAFDAC registration applies before scaling up.

blocks.title: Generators
blocks.text: Carbon monoxide from generator exhaust has no smell and can kill people sleeping or working nearby. Always run a generator outside, well away from doors, windows and vents, and never inside a shop, kitchen or house.
Inclusion and fairness

items: **Workers**: agree pay, hours and tasks in writing, pay on the agreed day, and give helpers safe working conditions.

**Customers**: treat every customer with respect, make your service usable for older customers and people with disabilities (for example, delivery or a phone order option), and give clear prices up front.
**Data**: under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, collect only the customer data you need, ask consent for marketing messages, and keep records secure.
**Opportunity**: when you hire, give fair consideration to women and young people in your community who need the work.

blocks.text: Handling a complaint well

items: Listen fully without interrupting or defending yourself.
Thank the customer for telling you; many unhappy customers simply leave without a word.
Agree a fair fix quickly: redo the job, replace the item or refund part of the price.
Write the complaint and its cause in your log the same day.
Change the standard or the training so the same problem does not repeat.

blocks.text: A complaint handled quickly and fairly often turns a customer into a loyal one, because it proves you care about getting things right.

Check your standard every few months. When you change a supplier, add a new product or hire a new helper, walk through the sheet again and update any step that no longer matches how the work is really done. An out-of-date standard is ignored quickly, so keep it short, current and pinned where the work happens.
Quality, safety and fairness are not extras for later. They are what make customers trust you with bigger orders, and what make good helpers stay.

takeaways: Write your quality standard so a helper can follow and check it.
Complaint rate = complaints ÷ orders × 100; track it monthly.
Use recognised safety practice for food, gas, electricity and money.
Fair pay, respectful service and careful data handling build trust.

activity.title: Create your quality sheet and complaint log
steps: Write the steps of your main product or service on one page.
Add a checkable standard to each step and mark the three most important.
Start a complaint log with columns: date, customer, problem, action, cause.
Calculate last month's complaint rate, even if roughly.
activity.evidence: A photo of your one-page quality standard and the first page of your complaint log.

lessons.title: A monthly dashboard: the six numbers that show real progress
objectives: Track six key numbers every month on one page
Calculate gross margin, net profit and repeat customer rate
Explain why profit and cash at hand can differ
Use a monthly review to decide one action

blocks.text: "Business is doing okay" is a feeling, not a measurement. A **dashboard** is one page where you write the same few numbers every month, so that you can see a trend and act early. Six numbers are enough for most small businesses.

head: Number
How to calculate
What it tells you
rows: Money in account and cash box
Whether you can pay next month's bills
Customers who bought again ÷ all customers × 100
Hours you worked on the business
Whether growth is costing your health and family time

blocks.title: The monthly review cycle
items: Record daily
Summarise monthly
Compare with last month
Decide one action
Act and record
blocks.caption: The same review every month turns records into decisions.

blocks.title: Worked example: Titi's three-month dashboard
blocks.context: For example, Titi tracks her egg business. Prices are approximate and for illustration: she sells at about ₦5,500 per crate, direct costs (mainly feed) are about ₦4,200 per crate, and fixed costs (helper, vaccines, transport, levies) are about ₦90,000 a month.
steps: Crates sold: Month 1 = 120, Month 2 = 135, Month 3 = 150.
Gross profit per crate: 5,500 − 4,200 = ₦1,300. Gross margin = 1,300 ÷ 5,500 × 100 = about 23.6 percent.
Net profit after ₦90,000 fixed costs: ₦66,000, ₦85,500, ₦105,000.
But in Month 3 the hotel still owes ₦180,000 for eggs delivered on credit, so her cash fell even though profit rose.
Repeat customers in Month 3: 18 of 24 customers bought again = 75 percent.
blocks.result: Titi's business is growing and profitable, but cash is the warning sign. Her one action for next month: agree with the hotel to pay every two weeks instead of monthly, and stop new credit above an agreed limit.

blocks.name: progress-tracking
blocks.alt: A person reviewing progress bars on a board
blocks.caption: Writing the same six numbers each month shows you the trend before it becomes a crisis.

blocks.text: Why profit and cash can differ

Profit counts sales when you make them. Cash counts money when it actually arrives. If customers buy on credit, if you pay suppliers in advance, or if you buy equipment, your cash can fall while profit rises. Many profitable small businesses close because they run out of cash. Watching both numbers side by side is the protection.
Simple tools for your dashboard

items: A notebook page with six rows and one column per month works perfectly.
Google Sheets on your phone can add up the numbers and draw a chart for you.
If you sell through Paystack, Opay or Moniepoint, download the monthly transaction history to check your revenue figure.
Keep receipts for big costs in one envelope or phone album so you can check costs too.

blocks.title: One action, not ten
blocks.text: At each monthly review, choose only one action based on the weakest number. Write it at the bottom of the dashboard and check it next month. Small, repeated improvements add up faster than big plans that never start.
Warning signs on a dashboard

items: Revenue rising but gross margin falling: input costs have gone up and your prices have not followed.
Net profit flat while revenue grows: fixed costs are growing too fast, or discounts are eating profit.
Repeat customer rate falling: check your complaint log; quality or reliability may be slipping.
Cash below one month of running costs: slow down spending and collect debts before anything else.
Owner hours rising every month: plan a handover before you burn out.

blocks.text: Compare each month with the month before and with the same month last year if you have it, because festive seasons, school fees periods and the rainy season change sales for many businesses. A fall in January after a busy December is normal; a fall that continues for three months is a signal to act.

Mark any estimate with a small letter E beside it. Estimates are acceptable at the start, but each month try to replace one estimate with a recorded figure. Within a few months your dashboard will rest on real records, and you will trust it enough to make decisions from it.

Track your owner hours too. If revenue rises but your hours rise faster, growth is being paid for with your rest and family time. That is a sign to look at delegation, which you will plan in Lesson 3.2.

takeaways: Track six numbers monthly: revenue, gross margin, net profit, cash, repeat rate and owner hours.
Gross margin shows what each sale contributes; net profit shows what the business earned.
Credit sales can make cash fall while profit rises.
End every review with one written action.

activity.title: Build your first dashboard
steps: Draw a table with the six numbers as rows and the last three months as columns.
Fill in each number using your records, estimating where you must and marking estimates.
Circle the weakest number or the worst trend.
Write one action for next month at the bottom of the page.
activity.evidence: A photo or screenshot of your completed three-month dashboard with one action written on it.

quiz.q: An order costs ₦60,000 in total. You want a 20 percent margin and the payment link charges 1.5 percent of the price. What should you quote, roughly?
quiz.explain: Price = 60,000 ÷ (1 − 0.20 − 0.015) = 60,000 ÷ 0.785 = about ₦76,433. ₦72,000 is a 20 percent markup on cost, which gives a margin below 20 percent and ignores the fee.

quiz.q: A customer sends a screenshot of a ₦120,000 transfer and asks you to release the order now. What should you do?
options: Release it because screenshots are proof
Check your own bank or wallet app and release only when the money shows there
Ask a friend whether the screenshot looks real
Release half the order
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Only money visible in your own account is confirmed.

quiz.q: Blessing processed 300 items and received 3 complaints. What is her complaint rate?
options: 3 percent
0.3 percent
10 percent
1 percent

quiz.q: Where should a generator be placed for a small shop?
options: Outdoors, away from doors, windows and vents
Inside the shop, near the door for security
In a closed store room to reduce noise
In the kitchen so it is easy to switch on
quiz.explain: Generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which has no smell and can kill. It must run outside, well away from openings.

quiz.q: Titi's profit rose for three months but her cash fell. What is the most likely cause from her dashboard?
options: Her gross margin collapsed
Her repeat customer rate fell
A large customer is buying on credit and paying late
She sold fewer crates
quiz.explain: Credit sales count as profit when made, but cash only arrives when the customer pays, so a late-paying customer drains cash.

modules.title: Grow With Discipline: Funding, Partnerships and Your 90-Day Plan
modules.overview: Now you turn your evidence into action. You will compare growth options and fund the best one safely, build partnerships and hand over tasks so the business no longer depends on you for everything, and finish with a 90-day growth plan that becomes your final project.

lessons.title: Choosing your next growth move and funding it safely
objectives: Compare growth options by effort and profit impact
Calculate the payback period of an investment
Test whether a loan repayment is affordable, including a bad-month scenario
Choose the safest funding source from savings, groups, cooperatives and lenders

blocks.text: Growth does not always mean a bigger shop or a big loan. It means more profit from a business that still runs well. Your diagnosis from Module 1 tells you your main limit; your dashboard from Module 2 tells you which numbers are weak. Now you choose **one** growth move that fixes the limit.
Five common growth moves

items: **Sell more to existing customers**: bigger packs, regular subscriptions, reminders before festive seasons.
**Reach new customers like your best ones**: use your customer profile to find more of the same people.
**Raise the price** where your quality and reliability justify it.
**Add capacity**: equipment, a helper or a better process so you can say yes to more orders.
**Add a product or service** that the same customers already ask for.

blocks.title: Effort versus profit impact
items: Quick wins: do first
Big bets: plan carefully
Small fixes: fit in
Avoid for now
blocks.caption: Start with high-impact, low-effort moves; plan big bets only with numbers.

blocks.text: Many owners jump to a big bet, such as a second shop, before trying the quick wins, such as asking each regular customer for a weekly standing order. Score each idea: how much extra monthly profit might it bring, and how much money and effort will it take?
Payback period

For any investment, calculate the **payback period**: cost of the investment ÷ extra monthly profit it brings. A short payback (a few months) is lower risk. A payback of several years for a small business is high risk, because things change.

blocks.title: Worked example: Aisha's second fryer
blocks.context: For example, in Lesson 1.1 Aisha found she refused about 3 orders a month because of her single fryer. A second fryer and gas burner would cost about ₦180,000 (approximate). Each extra order brings about ₦20,000 profit after all costs.
steps: Extra monthly profit: 3 orders × ₦20,000 = ₦60,000.
Payback period: ₦180,000 ÷ ₦60,000 = 3 months.
Option A, save first: putting aside ₦30,000 a month, she can buy it in 6 months with no debt.
Option B, a loan of ₦180,000 repaid at ₦36,000 a month for 6 months: total repaid ₦216,000, so the loan costs ₦36,000.
Affordability: ₦60,000 extra profit − ₦36,000 repayment = ₦24,000 a month left over.
Bad-month test: if only 2 extra orders come, extra profit is ₦40,000 and only ₦4,000 is left after repayment.
blocks.result: The loan is affordable only if the extra orders are reliable. Aisha chooses a middle path: she uses a cooperative loan for half the cost and her savings for the rest, so her monthly repayment is smaller and a slow month will not break her.

blocks.name: savings
blocks.alt: A person putting money into a savings jar
blocks.caption: Retained profit and group savings are often the safest first sources of growth money.

blocks.text: The funding ladder: safest first

head: Source
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Slower; needs discipline to keep it separate
Ajo, esusu, adashe or thrift groups
A planned lump sum on a known date
Join only groups with people you know and clear written rules
Read the by-laws, attend meetings, keep your contribution records
Ask for the total cost in naira, all fees and what happens if you pay late
Use only lenders registered with the FCCPC; avoid apps that demand access to your contacts
Never pay a fee to receive a grant; check only official websites

blocks.title: Loan and grant scams
blocks.text: Genuine grants do not ask you to pay a "processing fee" to an individual's account. Before using any digital lender, check that it appears on the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) list of approved digital lenders, and confirm government programmes, such as those from SMEDAN or the Bank of Industry, only on their official websites.
Raising your price as a growth move

A price increase can be the quickest win, because it needs no new equipment. If Titi raises her price from ₦5,500 to ₦5,800 per crate while costs stay the same, her gross profit per crate rises from ₦1,300 to ₦1,600. At 150 crates a month that is ₦45,000 more profit, even if she sells nothing extra. Give regular customers notice, explain the reason simply (for example, higher feed costs), and keep your quality steady.

Before signing any loan, ask the lender to write down the amount you receive, every fee, the total you will repay and the repayment dates. Compare the monthly repayment with the **extra** profit the loan will create, not with your total sales. Keep at least one month of running costs aside so a slow month does not force you to borrow again.

takeaways: Choose one growth move that fixes your main limit; try quick wins before big bets.
Payback period = investment cost ÷ extra monthly profit.
A loan is affordable only if extra profit covers the repayment, even in a slow month.
Climb the funding ladder from the safest source, and never pay to receive a grant.

activity.title: Test your growth move
steps: List three possible growth moves for your business.
Estimate the cost and extra monthly profit of each, and place them on the effort and impact matrix.
Calculate the payback period for your top choice.
If you need funding, compare two sources and run the bad-month test.
activity.evidence: A one-page growth decision sheet showing your matrix, payback calculation and chosen funding source.

lessons.title: Partnerships, delegation and building your support network
objectives: Decide which tasks to hand to a helper and calculate whether it pays
Write a task card and a simple work agreement
Identify partners who can bring customers, lower costs or give advice
Confirm partnership terms clearly in writing

blocks.text: A business that depends on the owner for every task cannot grow far, and the owner pays with her health and family time. Growth needs two kinds of help: **people who do tasks** for you and **partners who open doors**, such as suppliers, referrers, cooperatives and mentors.
What to delegate first

Delegate tasks that are repeatable, easy to check and take a lot of your hours. Keep the tasks that need your judgement: pricing, key customer relationships, quality checks and money decisions. Your owner-hours number from your dashboard shows where your time goes.

blocks.title: Handing over a task
items: List weekly tasks and hours
Pick a repeatable task
Write a task card
Train, watch and check
Hand over fully
blocks.caption: Delegation works when the standard is written and checked, not just explained once.

blocks.title: Worked example: Blessing hands over ironing
blocks.context: For example, Blessing's laundry now handles about 300 items a month. She irons everything herself at about 6 minutes per item. A helper would be paid about ₦100 per item ironed (approximate, for illustration).
steps: Time spent ironing: 300 items × 6 minutes = 1,800 minutes = 30 hours a month.
Cost of a helper: 300 × ₦100 = ₦30,000 a month.
Blessing uses the freed 30 hours to visit offices and sign 2 office contracts for weekly pickup.
Each office contract brings about ₦25,000 extra profit a month: 2 × ₦25,000 = ₦50,000.
Net gain: ₦50,000 − ₦30,000 = ₦20,000 more profit a month, plus a stronger business.
blocks.result: Delegating ironing pays because Blessing uses her freed time on work only she can do: winning and keeping bigger customers. Delegating without a plan for the freed hours would simply have cost her ₦30,000.

blocks.text: A task card and a simple agreement

items: **Task card**: the task name, the steps, what "done well" looks like, the safety rules and who to call with problems.
**Work agreement**: tasks, hours or pay per item, pay day, trial period, notice period, and rules on customer data and money.
Read the agreement together, give a copy, and keep one yourself; a WhatsApp message both of you reply to is better than nothing.

blocks.name: handshake-deal
blocks.alt: Two people shaking hands to agree a deal
blocks.caption: Clear written terms make partnerships and helper arrangements last.

blocks.text: Partners who open doors

head: Partner type
What they offer
Example
rows: Event planners recommending Aisha's small chops
Titi agreeing a fixed monthly feed order with one supplier
Five food sellers buying oil and flour together
A women's business association or the WODDI Good Mother Network (WGMN)
A tailor and a bead maker selling outfits with matching jewellery

blocks.text: Look for partners whose customers are the same as yours but who do not compete with you. For Aisha, event planners, cake makers and hall owners serve the same party clients. A referral partner may ask for a small commission, often agreed as a percentage of each order; write it down and pay it promptly to keep trust.

blocks.title: Confirm every deal in writing
blocks.text: After any partnership conversation, send a short message: "Thank you for today. To confirm: you will refer party clients to me, and I will pay 5 percent of each order you send, by transfer within 3 days of payment. Please reply OK if correct." This avoids misunderstandings later.
Communicating as a leader
Choosing and checking a helper

items: Ask for a reference from someone you trust, and give a paid trial of one or two weeks.
Start with tasks that do not involve handling large amounts of cash.
Check work against the task card daily at first, then weekly once quality is steady.
Pay on the agreed day without delay; reliability works both ways.

blocks.title: Worked example: buying oil together
blocks.context: For example, Aisha and four other food sellers in her area each use about 2 kegs of vegetable oil a month. Prices are approximate and for illustration.
steps: Buying alone, each pays about ₦38,000 per keg: 2 × ₦38,000 = ₦76,000 a month.
Buying 10 kegs together from a distributor, they are offered about ₦35,500 per keg.
Each seller now pays 2 × ₦35,500 = ₦71,000, saving ₦5,000 a month.
Shared transport for the 10 kegs costs ₦5,000 in total, or ₦1,000 each.
blocks.result: Each seller saves about ₦4,000 a month after transport, about ₦48,000 a year, as long as the group agrees in writing who collects the money and who keeps the receipts.

blocks.text: As your team and partners grow, communication becomes part of your job. Hold a short weekly check-in with helpers: what went well, what went wrong, what changes next week. Praise good work specifically. Correct mistakes privately and calmly, with reference to the task card. When you meet other women in business, share what you have learned; strong networks lift everyone in them.

takeaways: Delegate repeatable, checkable, time-heavy tasks; keep pricing, key customers and money decisions.
Delegation pays only when you use the freed hours on higher-value work.
Use a task card and a written agreement for every helper.
Find partners who share your customers but do not compete, and confirm terms in writing.

activity.title: Plan one handover and one partnership
steps: List your weekly tasks with the hours each takes.
Choose one task to delegate and write its task card.
Calculate the cost of delegating and what you will do with the freed hours.
Name one possible partner and draft the confirmation message you would send.
activity.evidence: Your task list with hours, one task card and one drafted partnership message.

lessons.title: Your 90-day growth plan and final project
objectives: Turn your growth move into one SMART 90-day goal
Break the goal into monthly targets and weekly actions
Choose leading and result measures to track
Assemble your final project from the work done in this course

blocks.text: Ninety days is long enough to see real results and short enough to stay focused. In this final lesson you bring everything together: your diagnosis, customer profile, canvas, costing, standards, dashboard, growth move and partnerships, into one plan you can follow on your phone or in a notebook.
Write one SMART goal

A SMART goal is **Specific** (what exactly), **Measurable** (a number), **Achievable** (stretching but realistic for your resources), **Relevant** (it fixes your main limit) and **Time-bound** (a date). "Grow my business" is not a goal. "Increase monthly items processed from 300 to 420 by 31 March, with a complaint rate under 1.5 percent" is.
Leading and result measures

A **result measure** shows whether you reached the goal, for example items processed or monthly profit. A **leading measure** is an action you control that drives the result, for example office visits made each week or follow-up messages sent. Track both: leading measures warn you early if you are falling behind.

blocks.title: The 90-day plan in four phases
items: Days 1-14: prepare
Days 15-45: launch
Days 46-75: adjust
Days 76-90: review
blocks.caption: Prepare tools and people first, launch, adjust using your numbers, then review honestly.

blocks.title: Worked example: Blessing's 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Blessing's main limit is time, and her customer profile shows that office workers value reliable pickup. Her growth move is office contracts plus a helper for ironing.
steps: Goal: increase items processed from 300 to 420 a month within 90 days, with a complaint rate under 1.5 percent.
Monthly targets: 340 items in Month 1, 380 in Month 2, 420 in Month 3, an increase of 40 items each month.
Days 1 to 14: recruit and train the ironing helper with a task card; print simple price cards for offices.
Days 15 to 45: visit 3 offices a week (leading measure) and offer a weekly pickup day.
Days 46 to 75: check the dashboard; if fewer than 2 offices have signed, ask receptionists who else to contact and ask current customers for referrals.
Days 76 to 90: compare all six dashboard numbers with the starting month and decide the next 90-day goal.
blocks.result: Each week Blessing knows exactly what to do and what to count. If items processed reach 420 with complaints under 1.5 percent, that is 6 complaints or fewer (420 × 1.5 ÷ 100 = 6.3), the goal is met.

blocks.name: goals
blocks.alt: A person standing beside a target with an arrow in the centre
blocks.caption: One clear goal with weekly actions turns a growth idea into results.

blocks.text: Risks and a weekly rhythm

items: Write the two biggest risks to your plan (for example, the helper leaves, or input prices rise) and one response for each.
Set one fixed weekly slot, such as Sunday evening for 30 minutes, to update your leading measures.
At the end of each month, update the dashboard and write one action.
Tell one trusted person, such as a mentor or a fellow member of your network, about your goal and agree to report progress to them.

blocks.text: Assemble your final project

items: Stage diagnosis with profit per hour (Lesson 1.1).
Customer profile with your interview tally (Lesson 1.2).
Business Model Canvas and readiness score (Lesson 1.3).
A full costing and quote for your core product or service (Lesson 2.1).
Quality standard, complaint log and three-month dashboard (Lessons 2.2 and 2.3).
Growth decision sheet, delegation plan and your 90-day plan (Module 3).

blocks.text: If you fall behind

Most plans fall behind somewhere. If your leading measure is on track but the result is not, your actions may be the wrong ones: go back to your customers and ask why. If the leading measure itself is behind, the problem is time or discipline: shrink the weekly action until you can do it every week. Change the plan on purpose, write the change down, and keep going. Abandoning a plan quietly is the most common way growth stops.
Using your plan with lenders and partners

Your final project is also a document you can show. A cooperative, microfinance bank or mentor will take you more seriously when you can show three months of dashboard numbers, a costed growth move with its payback period, and a plan for repaying any loan from extra profit. Keep a clean copy in a folder or a phone album, and update it every 90 days.

When the 90 days end, celebrate what worked, even if you did not reach the full target. Then start the next cycle: update your stage diagnosis, readiness score and canvas, compare them with your first versions from Module 1, and choose the next limit to fix. Steady 90-day cycles, repeated over a year, are how a stable business becomes a growing one.

blocks.title: Be honest in your project
blocks.text: Use your real numbers, marked as estimates where needed. A plan built on honest figures is far more useful to you, and to any lender, cooperative or mentor who reads it, than one that looks impressive but cannot be checked.

takeaways: One SMART goal that fixes your main limit beats many vague goals.
Track leading measures you control as well as the result you want.
Plan in four phases: prepare, launch, adjust, review.
Your final project gathers the real work you produced in every lesson.

activity.title: Write your 90-day plan
steps: Write one SMART goal and check it against all five letters.
Set a target for each of the three months.
Choose one leading measure and write the weekly actions for each phase.
List two risks with a response for each and set your weekly review time.
activity.evidence: Your one-page 90-day plan with goal, monthly targets, weekly actions, leading measure and risks.

quiz.q: A ₦240,000 freezer would bring about ₦40,000 extra profit a month. What is the payback period?
options: 4 months
6 months
8 months
10 months

quiz.q: A loan repayment is ₦36,000 a month and the investment adds about ₦40,000 profit in a slow month. What does the bad-month test tell you?
options: The loan is very safe
The loan should be twice as large
Only ₦4,000 is left in a slow month, so the plan is tight and needs a cushion
Repayments do not matter if sales are high
quiz.explain: ₦40,000 − ₦36,000 = ₦4,000. A thin cushion means a smaller loan, more savings or a reserve is wiser.

quiz.q: Someone offers you a government grant if you first pay a ₦15,000 processing fee into a personal account. What should you do?
options: Pay quickly before the slots fill up
Pay half now and half later
Ask friends whether they paid
Refuse and check the programme only on the official website
quiz.explain: Genuine grants do not ask for fees paid to a personal account. This is a common scam pattern.

quiz.q: Blessing pays a helper ₦30,000 a month for ironing. When does this delegation pay off?
options: When she uses the freed 30 hours to win work worth more than ₦30,000 in profit
Always, because helpers are cheap
Never, because she could do it herself
Only if the helper works for free in the first month
quiz.explain: Delegation pays when the owner spends the freed hours on higher-value work. Her office contracts brought ₦50,000, a ₦20,000 net gain.

quiz.q: Which is a leading measure for a goal of signing more office laundry clients?
options: Total monthly profit
Number of offices visited each week
Items processed last quarter
Complaint rate last year
quiz.explain: Office visits are an action she controls that drives the result. Profit and items processed are result measures.

finalQuiz.q: Which sign best shows a business is growth-ready rather than just stable?
options: She has a nice logo
She has known monthly profit for months and regularly refuses orders she cannot fill
She sells to friends and family
She works more hours than last year
finalQuiz.explain: Growth-ready means a stable base with records plus proven extra demand.

finalQuiz.q: A seller earns ₦48,000 profit in a month and works 80 hours. What is her profit per hour?
Which question best follows customer discovery principles?
options: Would you pay more for a premium version?
Don't you think my product is better?
What did you do the last time this problem happened?
Would you tell your friends about me?
finalQuiz.explain: It asks about real past behaviour rather than opinions or future promises.

finalQuiz.q: In the Business Model Canvas, which block answers 'Which suppliers or partners do I rely on?'
options: Channels
Customer Relationships
Key Activities
Key Partnerships
finalQuiz.explain: Key Partnerships lists the suppliers and partners the business depends on.

finalQuiz.q: An order costs ₦80,000. You want a 25 percent margin with no payment fee. What price gives that margin?
finalQuiz.explain: Price = 80,000 ÷ (1 − 0.25) = ₦106,667. ₦100,000 is a 25 percent markup on cost, which is only a 20 percent margin.

finalQuiz.q: Ingredients and packaging for an order cost ₦45,000. What is the minimum sensible deposit?
options: Nothing until delivery
₦45,000 or more
Only the delivery fee
finalQuiz.explain: A deposit should at least cover what you must buy in advance, so you never fund a client's order with your own cash.

finalQuiz.q: Which practice follows the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food?
options: Store raw meat above ready-to-eat food
Keep raw and cooked food separate
Reuse washing water to save money
Leave cooked food out all day for customers
finalQuiz.explain: Separating raw and cooked food is one of the five keys; the other options increase contamination risk.

finalQuiz.q: Revenue is ₦500,000 and direct costs are ₦350,000. What is the gross margin?
options: 70 percent
43 percent
15 percent
30 percent

finalQuiz.q: Profit is rising but cash at month end keeps falling. Which action best addresses this?
options: Tighten credit terms and ask large customers to pay more often
Cut the price to sell more
Stop recording credit sales
Take a loan to cover the gap every month
finalQuiz.explain: Falling cash with rising profit usually means money is stuck with debtors. Shorter, enforced credit terms bring cash in.

finalQuiz.q: Which growth move belongs in the 'quick wins' corner of the effort and impact matrix for most small sellers?
options: Opening a second shop in another city
Importing new machinery
Asking regular customers to set up weekly standing orders
Building a large factory
finalQuiz.explain: Standing orders from existing customers cost little and can add steady profit quickly.

finalQuiz.q: A digital loan app asks for access to all your phone contacts before approving a loan. What should you do?
options: Accept, since all apps do this
Accept, then delete the app later
Give the contacts of only close family
Decline and use only FCCPC-registered lenders or safer sources
finalQuiz.explain: Contact access is a warning sign linked to harassment of borrowers. Check registration and prefer safer funding sources.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the best SMART goal?
options: Grow my business this year
Increase weekly egg orders from 30 to 40 crates by 30 June, keeping complaints under 2 percent
Become the best caterer in town
Work harder and sell more
finalQuiz.explain: It is specific, measurable, realistic, relevant and has a date.

capstone.title: Small Business Growth Project
capstone.brief: Produce a growth file for your own business: an honest diagnosis, an evidence-based customer profile, an accurate costing and quote for your core product or service, a three-month dashboard, and a 90-day growth plan with funding and delegation decisions.
steps: Diagnose your stage and main limit with one month of real profit and profit-per-hour figures.
Interview at least 10 customers and write your customer profile with the tally.
Complete your Business Model Canvas and readiness score.
Cost and quote one full order or your core product, including your time and payment fees.
Write your quality standard, start a complaint log and fill a three-month dashboard.
Choose one growth move, calculate its payback and choose a funding source using the bad-month test.
Write your 90-day plan with a SMART goal, monthly targets, weekly actions, a delegation plan and two risks.
evidence: Stage diagnosis with profit per hour
Customer profile backed by at least 10 conversations
Business Model Canvas and readiness score
Costing sheet and written quote with deposit terms
Quality standard, complaint log and three-month dashboard
Growth decision sheet with payback and funding choice
One-page 90-day plan with leading measure and risks

sources.title: United Nations: Sustainable Development Goal 5, Gender equality
United Nations: Sustainable Development Goal 8, Decent work and economic growth
World Health Organization: Five keys to safer food
Nigeria Data Protection Commission (Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023)
Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria (SMEDAN)
